section.title: Sons and Heirs
section.sectionRationale: Paul deepens the argument from heirs to sonship. Once we were like children under guardians, enslaved to the basic principles of the world, but when the time had fully come God sent His Son, born of a woman, to redeem us and give us adoption as sons, and He sent the Spirit of His Son crying Abba, Father. Paul then pleads with the Galatians not to turn back to slavery, appealing to their former love for him.
section.thesis: In the fullness of time God sent His Son to redeem those under the law and make them sons, and sent the Spirit of His Son into their hearts crying Abba, Father, so that to turn back to law and the weak principles of the world is to abandon sonship for slavery, which is why Paul pleads with the Galatians in the anguish of a parent.
section.frameNote: Three movements: from slaves to sons, redeemed by the Son sent in the fullness of time and given the Spirit crying Abba; the folly of turning back to weak and worthless principles and observing days; and Paul's personal, pleading appeal as a spiritual parent in the pains of childbirth.

units.label: From slaves to sons
units.note: God sent His Son and the Spirit of His Son

verses.text: What I am saying is that as long as the heir is a child, he is no different from a slave, although he is the owner of everything.
He is subject to guardians and trustees until the date set by his father.
So also, when we were children, we were enslaved under the basic {{stoicheia|principles}} of the world.
But when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law,
to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our {{huiothesia|adoption as sons}}.
And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, “{{abba|Abba}}, Father!”
So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God.

units.label: Do not turn back to slavery
units.note: weak and worthless principles, observing days

verses.text: Formerly, when you did not know God, you were slaves to those who by nature are not gods.
But now that you know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you are turning back to those weak and worthless principles? Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?
You are observing special days and months and seasons and years!
I fear for you, that my efforts for you may have been in vain.

units.label: Paul's pleading appeal
units.note: the anguish of a spiritual parent

verses.text: I beg you, brothers, become like me, for I became like you. You have done me no wrong.
You know that it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you.
And although my illness was a trial to you, you did not despise or reject me. Instead, you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself.
What then has become of your blessing? For I can testify that, if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.
Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth?
Those people are zealous for you, but not in a good way. Instead, they want to isolate you from us, so that you may be zealous for them.
Nevertheless, it is good to be zealous if it serves a noble purpose, at any time, and not only when I am with you.
My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is {{morphoo|formed}} in you,
how I wish I could be with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.

stoicheia.gloss: The basic principles or elemental things, the ABCs of the world. The term can refer to elementary religious rules or to the spiritual powers behind them. Paul uses it for the whole realm of law and ritual religion that enslaves before Christ, and shockingly he groups a return to the law with the old pagan bondage: both are weak and worthless compared to sonship in Christ.

huiothesia.gloss: Adoption as sons, the legal act of placing someone as a full son with all the rights of an heir. God redeemed those under the law precisely so they might receive adoption. This is not merely forgiveness but the granting of family status: the redeemed are made sons and daughters of God, with full standing and a sure inheritance.

abba.gloss: Abba, the Aramaic word for father, the intimate address a child uses at home. The Spirit of the Son prompts believers to cry Abba, Father, the same word Jesus used in Gethsemane. It marks the tender, confident access of a child to a loving father, the opposite of the fear and distance of a slave under law.

morphoo.gloss: To form, to shape, to bring to full form, as an embryo takes shape in the womb. Paul longs for Christ to be formed in the Galatians, for the character and life of Christ to take full shape within them. He pictures himself again in the pains of childbirth until this happens, showing that the goal of the gospel is not mere decision but Christ fully formed in the believer.

basic.context: Paul pictures the difference between a child who is still like a slave and a grown son who inherits. He says that before Christ we were like minors, enslaved under religious rules. But at the right time God sent His Son to redeem us and make us sons, and He sent the Spirit so we can call God Abba, Father. To go back to law now is to trade sonship for slavery, and Paul pleads with them not to do it.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage combines rich doctrine, the sending of the Son and the Spirit, with raw pastoral emotion. Notice the movement from slaves to sons to heirs, and then the personal appeal. Read the doctrine and the pleading together: Paul argues because he loves them like a parent.
basic.originalLanguages: Before Christ we were enslaved under the stoicheia, the basic principles of the world. God sent His Son to give us huiothesia, adoption as sons, and sent the Spirit so we cry abba, Father, the intimate word for daddy. Paul longs for Christ to be morphoo, formed, fully shaped in them.
basic.typology: The fullness of time fulfills the long waiting of the Old Testament for the promised deliverer. God sending His Son, born of a woman, echoes the promise of the seed of the woman in Genesis. Adoption as sons fulfills Israel's calling as God's son, now extended to all who are in Christ.
basic.christ: God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law. Christ enters our condition fully, keeps the law, and pays the price to make us sons. The Spirit He gives is the Spirit of His Son. Christ's sonship becomes the pattern and ground of ours, so that we share His cry, Abba, Father.
basic.god: God is the Father who sends both the Son and the Spirit, and who adopts slaves into His family as sons and heirs. He acts at just the right time, according to His plan. He is the one who knows us, verse 9, before we know Him. The whole passage reveals the heart of a Father who brings us near.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8 speaks of the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry Abba, Father. John 1 says those who receive Christ are given the right to become children of God. Ephesians 1 says God predestined us for adoption through Christ.
basic.oneStory: The story moves from slavery to sonship. What Israel foreshadowed as God's son, and what humanity lost in Eden, is restored and surpassed in Christ. God sends His Son to redeem and His Spirit to assure, gathering a family who call Him Father, and to return to slavery would be to undo the gospel.

context.literary:
The passage has two halves with a hinge between them. Verses 1 to 7 give an analogy and its application, and verses 8 to 20 turn that doctrine into a personal appeal. The hinge is verse 8, where the 'we' and 'our' of verses 3 to 6 give way to 'you,' and the abstract picture becomes the Galatians' own biography. The two verbs 'formerly' and 'now' in verses 8 and 9 carry the turn, and what Paul says about their past, ignorant slavery makes the present drift seem all the stranger.

Within verses 1 to 7 there is a careful sequence. The child heir is like a slave, verse 1, held under guardians, verse 2, so also 'we' were enslaved, verse 3. Then comes the great reversal with 'But when the time had fully come,' verse 4. The sending of the Son in verses 4 and 5 and the sending of the Spirit in verse 6 are set in parallel, and the same Greek verb is used for each act. The unit closes on a shift in pronoun that moves from 'we' to 'you' in the singular: 'you are no longer a slave, but a son,' verse 7. The doctrine is intended to be heard by each reader as personal.

The second half shifts tone. The questions of verses 9 and 15 and 16 show a mind torn between anger and affection. Paul writes in short sentences that break off, and in verse 20 he admits that he cannot find the right register: 'change my tone.' The imperative of verse 12, 'become like me,' is the only direct command in the section. The central image of verse 19, a mother in labour, is a surprise, since Paul has been writing as a father. It gathers the whole of the pastoral appeal into one picture of costly love, and it prepares for the allegory of Hagar and Sarah that follows, where the mother is the issue.
context.historical:
The household image of verses 1 and 2 reflects arrangements familiar to Paul's readers, whether Greek, Roman or Jewish. A young heir, though destined to own the estate, lived under the authority of guardians and household managers until the age his father had fixed. The details of such arrangements varied from place to place, and Paul does not need them to be uniform. The picture of an heir who in practice lives like a servant was a common one. The point is that the father, not the guardians, decides when it ends.

The word for adoption, huiothesia, belonged to the Greco-Roman world, where a family without a son could adopt one, giving him the legal standing of a natural child, the family name and the right to inherit. The Roman practice was formal, and an adopted son stood in law as though he had been born into the family. For Gentile readers this was close to home. Paul uses it to say that what was foreign to them by birth has been made theirs by the Father's act.

The 'basic principles of the world' and the 'special days and months and seasons and years' of verse 10 may allude to the Jewish calendar of Sabbaths, new moons, festivals and sabbatical years, as in Colossians 2:16. Some also think that pagan observances, including astrology, played a part in the Galatians' past, since verse 8 speaks of their service to those who 'by nature are not gods.' Paul says in Romans 14:5-6 that special days are a matter of conviction among believers, so his alarm here must be about days as a ground of standing before God.

The personal story of verses 13 and 14 remembers Paul's first visit, when sickness delayed or redirected him. The Galatians welcomed him warmly, and the language 'as if I were an angel of God' recalls the scene at Lystra in Acts 14:11-15 where the crowds took Paul and Barnabas for gods. The 'trial' in his body, whatever it was, could have invited contempt in a culture that read illness as a sign of divine disfavour, and the Galatians did not despise him.
context.canonical:
The sonship in verses 4 to 7 is the fulfilment of a theme that begins with the exodus. God told Pharaoh that Israel was His firstborn son, Exodus 4:22-23, and Hosea 11:1 looks back on the nation as a child called out of Egypt. Matthew 2:15 applies the same line to the infant Jesus, showing that the true Son took up Israel's story. Paul's thought is that the Son who is faithful where Israel failed shares His sonship with those who are in Him.

The sending of the Son 'born of a woman' picks up Genesis 3:15 and the promise of the woman's seed. The Spirit who cries 'Abba' recalls the prayer of Jesus in Gethsemane, Mark 14:36. The parallel text is Romans 8:14-17, which says that those led by the Spirit are sons of God and have received a Spirit of adoption by whom we cry 'Abba, Father.' John 1:12-13 and Ephesians 1:5 give the same truth in the gospel and in Paul's praise.

Verses 8 to 11 find their echoes in 1 Corinthians 8:4-6, where idols are said to be nothing in the world and there is one God, and in Colossians 2:16-23, where days, festivals and 'the basic principles of the world' are called a shadow of what is to come. Paul's personal pleading recalls his gentle care for the Thessalonians as a nursing mother, 1 Thessalonians 2:7-8, and his claim to be a father through the gospel, 1 Corinthians 4:15.

The goal in verse 19, that Christ be formed in believers, links to Romans 8:29, where they are predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, and to 2 Corinthians 3:18, where beholding the Lord they are transformed into His image. The inheritance of verse 7 finds its end in Revelation 21:7.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Galatians to measure their situation by something they cannot dispute, the fact that they cry 'Abba, Father.' He knows that rival teachers have offered them more religion, in the form of rules and calendars. He answers by pointing out what they already have, the Spirit of the Son in their hearts, and by asking why anyone would trade it for the nursery rules of an earlier stage.

The analogy of the child heir is built to carry a specific argument. The Galatians were being told that to become mature in faith they must adopt the law, and Paul turns that around: the law and the world's principles belonged to a time of minority. Growing up means coming into the freedom of sons, and a return to the rules would be a return to childhood. In this way he reverses the rival teachers' claim that the law brings maturity.

The second half is a deliberately emotional appeal. Paul has argued the doctrine in chapters 3 and 4, and now he reminds them of the bond between them: the welcome they gave him, the affection they showed, his own willingness to become like them. He wants them to see that his bluntness comes from love and that the rival teachers' attention comes from something else. Verse 17 says that their zeal is meant to shut the Galatians out from Paul and his companions so that they will seek those teachers. His final wish is not for their agreement but for Christ to take shape in them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The sending of the Son and the Spirit is a description of what God has done, in history and in each believer, and it is the ground of everything else the passage says. It is not a command. The imperative that does appear is the plea of verse 12, 'become like me,' and it is Paul's personal appeal as the Galatians' apostle, not a general call to imitate any teacher. In Paul's case the point is that he gave up his own Jewish privileges to live as a Gentile among Gentiles, and he asks them to be as free of the law as he is.

The description of the Galatians' welcome, including their readiness to give up their eyes, is a record of their warmth and not a prescription for how churches should treat a visiting preacher. What does carry over is the standard that truth should be honoured even when it comes with an unattractive messenger.

The observance of days and seasons raises a question of application. Paul condemns the Galatians' practice, but in Romans 14:5-6 he allows each to be convinced in his own mind about a special day. The difference is the basis: in Galatia the days were being treated as a requirement for standing with God, while in Romans they are a matter of conscience that must not divide the church. The passage therefore does not forbid all calendars or church seasons, but it does forbid making them the grounds of acceptance.

The cry 'Abba, Father' describes the Spirit's work in every believer and may be used as an assurance. It is not a formula that makes prayer work.

debates.question: Who or what are the 'basic principles of the world' in verses 3 and 9?

views.label: Elementary religious teaching
views.case: The Greek word stoicheia first meant things in a row, such as the letters of the alphabet, and so came to mean basics or first principles. On this reading the 'principles' are the elementary lessons of religion for the childhood of humanity, including the Jewish law for the Jews and pagan religion for the Gentiles. The phrase 'weak and worthless' in verse 9 fits a childish stage.

views.label: Spiritual powers behind the world
views.case: The BSB footnote gives 'elemental forces' as an alternative. Some take the term to mean the spirit beings or powers believed to rule the world, which pagan worship served, verse 8, 'those who by nature are not gods.' On this view Paul sees both pagan worship and law-keeping as bondage to the same hostile order.

views.label: The physical elements
views.case: Others take the words to mean the elements of the physical world, earth, air, fire and water, which were the objects of pagan worship and the basis of the calendar of days and seasons that Paul mentions in verse 10.

debates.bearing: Paul places Jew and Gentile alike under the same word, 'we' in verse 3 and 'you' in verse 8. Whatever the term means, he is saying that life without Christ, whether under the law or under idols, is a slavery from which the Son has redeemed us.

debates.question: Does the Spirit come because we are sons, or make us sons?

views.label: The Spirit confirms an existing sonship
views.case: Verse 6 begins, 'And because you are sons,' which can be read as saying that sonship comes first and the sending of the Spirit follows. On this reading sonship is received by faith in the Son and the Spirit applies and confirms it, so that the believer cries 'Abba.'

views.label: The Spirit is the means by which sonship is realised
views.case: Romans 8:15 speaks of 'the Spirit of adoption,' by whom we cry 'Abba.' Others therefore stress that the Spirit is the one who brings believers into the family and gives them the filial heart. The sequence is logical, not temporal, and both belong together.

debates.bearing: Paul gives no hint that anyone is a son without the Spirit or has the Spirit without being a son. The two come together at conversion, as 3:2 and 3:26 indicate, and the point of verse 6 is the assurance that the cry of the heart proves the status.

debates.question: What was Paul's illness in verses 13 and 14?

views.label: A bodily weakness of unknown kind
views.case: Paul says only that it was an illness and a trial to the Galatians. The text does not name it, and Paul speaks elsewhere of a thorn in the flesh, 2 Corinthians 12:7-9, without saying what it was. This is the cautious reading and leaves the question open.

views.label: An eye complaint
views.case: Verse 15 speaks of the Galatians giving their eyes, and 6:11 refers to the large letters Paul writes. Some conclude that his illness affected his sight. Others reply that giving one's eyes was a proverbial way of saying one would give something very dear.

debates.bearing: The point of the passage does not depend on the diagnosis. What matters is that Paul preached in weakness, that the Galatians welcomed him in spite of it, and that this shows the truth of his message.

study.originalLanguages:
The phrase 'when the time had fully come' in verse 4 contains the noun pleroma, fullness, from the verb to fill. The time is a measure that has filled up, as a vessel fills, and the word stands in contrast to the date set by the father in verse 2. God had set a date and when the date arrived He acted. The word for time here is chronos, a span of time, and the thought is that the whole period of waiting reached its full measure. Paul uses the same verb of sending in two places, exapostello in verse 4 and again in verse 6. The prefix means 'out from,' and the verb is used of a commissioned messenger sent out from the one who sends. The Son is sent out from the Father, and the Spirit of the Son is sent out from God, in two matching missions.

In verse 4 the Son is described as 'born of a woman, born under the law,' using two participles of ginomai, 'to become, to come to be.' It means that He came to be, entered into, a human mother's womb and the law's jurisdiction. Paul chooses a verb of entering a condition, and does not use a verb of simple birth. The purpose in verse 5 is a double one, to redeem those under the law and to receive adoption, and the second purpose clause says that the redemption is a means to the family.

The verb for 'crying' in verse 6, krazo, is a strong verb for a loud and urgent call, used of the cry of the afflicted. Its participle is neuter, agreeing with 'Spirit,' so that it is the Spirit who cries in our hearts, while in Romans 8:15 it is 'we' who cry by the Spirit. Both are true, and Paul puts the weight in each place on the Spirit's initiative and our voice.

In verse 9 there is a deliberate reversal. 'Now that you know God, or rather are known by God' uses the same verb of knowing twice, first active and then passive. Paul corrects himself: the primary fact is not their knowledge of God but God's knowledge of them, a knowing that is also a choosing. In verse 10 'observing' is the verb paratereo, to watch closely and scrupulously, as one watches a calendar for the right day. In verse 17, 'isolate' is from ekkleio, 'to shut out,' and the plan of the rivals is to shut the Galatians out from Paul so that they will come to depend on them. In verse 19 the 'pains of childbirth' are from the verb odino, which describes the pangs of labour. And in verse 20 the plea to 'change my tone' means to alter his voice, a wish to be present so that the right tone can be found.

typology.type: Israel as God's firstborn son, Exodus 4:22-23
typology.fulfillment: God called Israel His son and demanded Pharaoh let him go to serve Him. Hosea 11:1 recalls that He loved Israel as a child and called His son out of Egypt, and Matthew 2:15 applies the line to Jesus. In Christ the sonship that Israel only partly lived is lived perfectly, and Galatians 4:5-6 says it is shared with all who are in Him. The correspondence is of redemption from slavery for sonship. The type falls short because Israel's sonship was national and often broken, while the sonship in Christ is personal and secured.

typology.type: The seed of the woman, Genesis 3:15
typology.fulfillment: The promise in Eden of a seed of the woman who would crush the serpent is the oldest promise of a deliverer, and 'born of a woman' in Galatians 4:4 recalls it. The pattern is of a human champion for a human problem. In Christ the promise is fulfilled in a way that goes beyond any expectation, since the one born of a woman is also the Son sent from God. Hebrews 2:14-15 says that He shared in flesh and blood to destroy the one who holds the power of death. The type is still working out, since the final defeat of the serpent comes at the end.

typology.type: The Son who cries Abba, Mark 14:36
typology.fulfillment: In Gethsemane Jesus prayed 'Abba, Father,' submitting His will to the Father's. The Spirit who cries the same words in believers makes them sharers in the Son's own relation to the Father. Romans 8:15-17 draws the link, adding that we are heirs with Christ if we share His sufferings. The pattern is of a prayer that trusts and obeys. What is new in us is that the cry is given and not achieved. The type is limited in that Jesus prayed from a unique sonship, and we pray from an adopted one.

Israel's calendar of Sabbaths, new moons and festivals gave rhythm to the life of the nation and pointed forward. Colossians 2:16-17 calls them a shadow of what was to come, and Hebrews 4:9-10 speaks of a Sabbath rest that still remains for God's people. In Christ the substance has arrived. To keep the days as a requirement is to cling to the shadow when the reality is present. The type is not despised, since Paul allows days to be kept as a matter of conscience, Romans 14:5-6, but it cannot be a ground for standing before God.

study.christ:
The central claim of the passage is that God sent His Son, and the whole of the redemption turns on who the Son is. The verb of sending implies that He was with the Father before He came, and the two descriptions that follow, 'born of a woman, born under the law,' say how far He came. He took on the same humanity as the people He came to save and put Himself under the same law that held them. He is not a distant rescuer but one who enters the condition of those He redeems. This is the same movement that Philippians 2:6-8 describes, from equality with God to the form of a servant and obedience to death.

The purpose of His coming has two steps. He redeems those under the law, which is to say that He pays the price and breaks the hold of the old order, and the result is that they receive adoption. The redemption is not an end in itself. It leads to a family. Christ's own sonship is the pattern and the ground of ours, so that Paul can say that God sent 'the Spirit of His Son' into our hearts. Believers do not merely have a new status; they share the Son's relationship, and the Father hears them as He hears Him. Hebrews 2:11 says that He is not ashamed to call them brothers.

The final lines of the passage show the aim of the Christian life as Christ being formed in us, verse 19. The word 'formed' speaks of a likeness growing in a person, as a child takes shape before birth. It is not about imitating a good example from outside; it is the Son's character being worked into the believer by the Spirit. In 2 Corinthians 3:18 the same process is described as being changed from glory to glory into His image.

A guard against forced allegory is needed here. Paul does not claim that the guardians and trustees of verse 2 are allegorical figures for particular persons, and he does not turn the details of the household into a hidden code. The analogy is made to say one thing: that the time of waiting was real, ended by the Father's decision, and that the Son's coming marked the end. The reader should take the analogy as far as Paul takes it and no farther.
study.god:
God appears in this passage as a Father who has a plan and keeps to its timing. The 'date set by his father' of verse 2 is picked up by 'the time had fully come' of verse 4. Nothing in the history of redemption is accidental. The long waiting under law and the world's principles was not a delay caused by a failed plan but a stage in the Father's purpose. That is a comfort to those who wonder why God allows long waits, for it says that the date is His and that He will keep it.

He is also a God who sends. The Father sends the Son and then sends the Spirit of the Son, so that in this one passage the whole Trinity is at work in the rescue of sinners. The Father plans and sends, the Son comes and redeems, and the Spirit applies and assures. The doctrine of God that comes out of this is not abstract: it is a picture of three persons acting in agreement for the sake of a family. Each act is complete, and each depends on the others. The Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son, which says that He is bound to the Son and brings the Son's own life to believers.

The passage also shows a God who knows His people before they know Him. 'Known by God' is the better description of the Christian life than 'knowing God,' because it places the initiative where it belongs. Our hold on Him is weaker than His hold on us. Paul wants the Galatians to feel the force of that, since a person who is known and loved by God has no reason to go back to powers that are not gods.

For worship, the passage invites a particular posture. Believers address God as Father, with the confidence of children who are sure of their welcome, and with the reverence that the word 'Father' carries. The cry 'Abba' is both close and respectful. The God who adopts slaves into His family does not do it reluctantly. He sends His own Son and His own Spirit, and He makes heirs of those who had no claim. To lose sight of that is what the Galatians were in danger of doing, and the passage is meant to restore it.

crossReferences.note: God calls Israel His firstborn son and tells Pharaoh to let him go. It is the first sounding of the sonship theme that Paul takes up, and it shows that redemption from slavery was always meant to lead to sonship.

The prophet recalls that when Israel was a child God loved him and called His son out of Egypt. It gives the background to the idea of Israel as a child under care, which Paul uses in the picture of the child heir.
Jesus prays 'Abba, Father' in Gethsemane. It is the only place in the gospels where the Aramaic word is recorded on His lips, and the Spirit's cry in Galatians 4:6 shares His own words.
The nearest parallel to Galatians 4:4-7, where those led by the Spirit are sons, receive a Spirit of adoption and cry Abba, and are heirs with Christ if they share His sufferings.
To those who receive Him, Christ gave the right to become children of God, born of God and not of human will. It sets sonship as a gift from above, in the same way as Galatians 4:5.
God chose us before the foundation of the world and predestined us for adoption through Jesus Christ. It shows that the sonship of Galatians 4 was part of the Father's plan from before time.

Paul warns against judgments about festivals, new moons and Sabbaths, which are a shadow of what is to come, and against submitting to the basic principles of the world. It is a close companion to Galatians 4:9-10.
Idols are nothing in the world, and for us there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. It matches Paul's description in Galatians 4:8 of those who by nature are not gods.

One person considers one day more sacred, and another considers every day alike, and each should be fully convinced. It shows that Galatians 4:10 is not a ban on every calendar but on days as a requirement.
Paul's thorn in the flesh, and the Lord's answer that His grace is sufficient. It helps to read Galatians 4:13-14 as a picture of a man whose weakness did not hinder the gospel.
Paul says he was gentle among them like a nursing mother and shared not only the gospel but his own self. It is the same pastoral voice that speaks in Galatians 4:19.

Paul tells the Corinthians that though they have countless guides in Christ they have not many fathers, since he became their father through the gospel. It parallels the parent language of Galatians 4:19.
Those whom God foreknew He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son. It states the goal that Paul has in view when he longs for Christ to be formed in the Galatians.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible can be told as a movement from slavery to sonship. Adam was made as God's image and son, Luke 3:38, and lost his place through the fall. Israel was redeemed from Egypt as God's firstborn son, but the nation proved unfaithful, and the prophets looked for a day when God would give His people a new heart and put His Spirit within them. Galatians 4 declares that the day has come. The Son was sent, the price was paid, and the Spirit was given, and the whole of the long history now has its answer.

What this passage answers from before is the question of why the long waiting. God had made a promise to Abraham and had given a law, and yet the world remained under slavery. Paul says that the waiting was like the minority of an heir, appointed by the Father, and that the date arrived. It also answers the question of what happened to the sonship lost in Eden. In Christ the true Son enters the human condition and lifts those who are in Him into the family.

What it sets up is the rest of the letter and of the New Testament. The allegory of Hagar and Sarah in the next verses will show the two ways of living, as slaves or as children of the free woman. The fruit of the Spirit in chapter 5 will show what the life of sons looks like. And Paul's longing that Christ be formed in them points toward the final transformation, when believers will be like Him, 1 John 3:2.

The story ends in the new creation, where the adoption is complete and the inheritance is received. Romans 8:23 says that we wait eagerly for our adoption, the redemption of our bodies, though we already have the Spirit as a firstfruit. Revelation 21:7 says that the one who conquers will inherit these things, and God will be his God and he will be His son. The slaves have become sons, the sons have become heirs, and the Father's house is full.

sermon.title: From Slavery to Sonship (Galatians 4:1 to 11)
sermon.why: Begg traces the move from slavery under the elementary principles to full sonship secured by the sending of the Son and the Spirit, and warns against turning back to bondage after being made sons and heirs of God.

quiz.q: What did God do when the time had fully come?

options.text: He sent His Son, born of a woman, to redeem us and make us sons.
options.note: Verses 4 and 5 state the sending of the Son and our adoption.

options.text: He gave a new and stricter law to keep.
options.note: He sent His Son to redeem those under the law, not a new law.

options.text: He left humanity to find its own way to Him.
options.note: God took the initiative by sending His Son.

options.text: He abandoned the promise to Abraham.
options.note: The sending of the Son fulfills the promise, not abandons it.

quiz.q: What shows that believers are truly sons of God?

options.text: God sent the Spirit of His Son into their hearts, crying Abba, Father.
options.note: Verse 6 makes the Spirit the seal of sonship.

options.text: Their careful observance of special days.
options.note: The Spirit, not calendar keeping, marks sonship.

options.text: Their descent from Abraham by birth.
options.note: Sonship comes through Christ and the Spirit, not physical descent.

options.text: Their perfect obedience to the law.
options.note: Sonship is God's gift, sealed by the Spirit, not earned by law.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the Galatians turning to law observance?

options.text: As turning back to weak and worthless principles and slavery.
options.note: Verse 9 calls it a return to bondage.

options.text: As a wise step forward in maturity.
options.note: Paul sees it as a step backward into slavery, not forward.

options.text: As a harmless matter of personal taste.
options.note: He fears his labor among them may be in vain, so it is not harmless.

options.text: As proof of their strong faith.
options.note: It endangers their faith rather than proving it.

quiz.q: What is Paul's aim for the Galatians in verse 19?

options.text: That Christ would be fully formed in them.
options.note: Paul labors like a parent until Christ is formed in them.

options.text: That they would simply feel more religious.
options.note: The goal is Christ formed in them, not mere religious feeling.

options.text: That they would become loyal to Paul personally.
options.note: His aim is Christ in them, not personal loyalty to himself.

options.text: That they would keep the calendar more strictly.
options.note: He wants Christ formed in them, not law observance.

quiz.q: What does adoption as sons give the believer?

options.text: Full family standing as a son and heir through God.
options.note: Verse 7 moves from son to heir through God.

options.text: A temporary status that must be renewed by works.
options.note: Adoption grants permanent family standing, not a status earned by works.

options.text: The right to look down on others.
options.note: Sonship humbles and unites; it is not a badge of superiority.

options.text: Nothing until the law is fully kept.
options.note: Sonship and inheritance are God's gift, received in Christ.

questions: The Spirit prompts you to cry Abba, Father. How does knowing God as an intimate Father, not a distant master, change the way you pray?
Paul says returning to law is a return to slavery. What rules or performance are you tempted to trust for your standing with God?
You are known by God before you ever knew Him. How does resting in God's knowing love steady you when your feelings waver?
Paul labors until Christ is formed in the Galatians. What would it look like for Christ to be more fully formed in your character this year?
Paul risked being seen as an enemy by telling the truth in love. Who in your life might need you to speak hard truth out of genuine love?

translationNotes.note: Basic principles renders stoicheia, the elementary things or elemental forces, as the BSB footnote notes; Paul applies it to enslaving religion, whether pagan ritual or law kept for justification.
Abba is the Aramaic word for father, retained in the Greek text; it conveys the intimate, trusting address of a child, the same word Jesus used in Gethsemane.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Galatians 4:1-20. wording is unchanged. Sermon verified this session from the Truth For Life series A Study in Galatians, Volume 1 by Alistair Begg; the movement spans 4:1-20 while the sermon covers 4:1-11, the sonship core of the passage.
